anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: A static mismatch between the physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of statistics or optimizer choice.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same data or metadata objects, producing wait chains or deadlocks that stall or abort workload execution.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes collectively saturate host CPU, driving run-queue growth, context switching, and broad latency inflation independent of any single SQL statement.

When all three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits an intertwined failure pattern: queries perform full scans or non-covering index lookups that touch many rows, inflating the lock footprint and holding row/page/table locks far longer than expected. The enlarged critical sections create dense blocker–waiter trees and frequent deadlocks, while the excessive I/O and predicate evaluation work drives CPU utilization toward saturation. Under high CPU load, the lock manager itself slows, lengthening detection and wake-up cycles, so blocking and deadlock resolution take longer. Applications see sharp spikes in response times, timeouts, and retry storms; monitoring shows near-max CPU usage, long lock-wait queues, repeated deadlock victim messages, and plan shapes dominated by scans that could be selective with proper indexing.

Causally, poor schema and index design is the initiating factor: missing or non-covering indexes force broad data access, which increases the number and duration of locks acquired. The prolonged locks raise the probability of collisions and deadlocks, producing Transaction Lock Contention. As sessions wait, blocked tasks may still consume CPU through spin-loops or wake-ups, while unblocked sessions keep issuing inefficient scans, jointly driving a CPU Resource Anomaly. Elevated CPU usage slows lock acquisition, latch operations, and deadlock detection, further extending transaction lifetimes and deepening contention. The feedback loop—inefficient access ➔ longer locks ➔ higher contention ➔ CPU saturation ➔ slower lock processing—amplifies each symptom until overall OLTP throughput collapses.

entry.official_definition: The number of seconds the server waits for activity on an interactive connection before closing it.
entry.trigger_condition: An interactive session remains idle longer than interactive_timeout.
entry.workload_impact: The server closes the idle interactive connection.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
